title: Migration systems built around return are confronting ageing, multigenerational settlement, and cross-border social-protection gaps
source_unit: ILO STREAM, Old-age security in the South Asia–Gulf migration corridor: policy challenges and opportunities, and accompanying ILO article
geography: South Asia–Gulf Cooperation Council migration corridor, focused on lower- and middle-income Indian migrant families with long residence in the United Arab Emirates

observations.period: 2026; long-term migrant ageing and the end of temporary-migration assumptions

denominator.unit: ILO STREAM research paper focused on long-term Indian migrant families in the UAE

migration_duration.value: many migrant workers spend decades in the Gulf and some families have children and grandchildren born and raised there

policy_mismatch.value: migration and social-protection systems built around eventual return increasingly struggle to fit long-term and multigenerational lives in the destination

life_course.value: retirement, care, housing, residency and family continuity become part of migration policy rather than a separate post-migration issue

observations.method: Independent research paper invited within the ILO STREAM Voices and Insights series, drawing on more than a decade of research with migrant families; it is a focused qualitative and policy analysis, not a population prevalence study.
observations.uncertainty: The paper focuses on Indian families in the UAE and does not establish how common the same arrangements are across all nationalities, occupations, Gulf states, or income groups.
observations.subgroup: Long-term and lower- or middle-income migrant workers, retirees, adult children, multigenerational families, women and dependants, employers, origin-country communities, and destination-country institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some workers may prefer return migration or maintain viable transnational family strategies; long residence does not by itself imply a right or desire to settle permanently in the destination.

observations.period: 2026; retirement income security for long-term migrant workers

denominator.unit: ILO paper’s retirement-security analysis for lower- and middle-income Indian migrant families in the UAE

income_sources.value: many workers rely on end-of-service indemnity, personal savings and family support rather than comprehensive pension systems

adequacy_risk.value: the paper describes these sources as limited, unpredictable, or inadequate for long-term retirement security

cross_border_gap.value: protection gaps arise across destination and origin systems when contributions, employment histories, or benefits do not travel with the worker

observations.method: Research and policy synthesis centered on migrant-family experiences and institutional arrangements; no representative income-replacement estimate is claimed here.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not produce a harmonized national measure of retirement adequacy, contribution histories, household wealth, or the relative importance of savings, indemnity, pensions, remittances, and family support.
observations.subgroup: Lower-paid and less-protected workers, workers with interrupted employment, women and dependants, older migrants, families supporting retirees, and workers outside bilateral social-security agreements.
observations.counterinterpretation: End-of-service payments and private savings may provide meaningful security for some households, and family support can function as a chosen social institution rather than only a failed public pension substitute.

observations.period: 2026; retirement healthcare, housing, and residency security

denominator.unit: ILO paper’s later-life security analysis for long-term migrant residents in the Gulf

healthcare.value: affordable and comprehensive healthcare becomes harder to access after retirement, especially when employer-provided coverage ends

housing.value: housing and care costs can make ageing in the Gulf financially difficult for lower-income retirees

residency.value: visa extensions and residence pathways may depend on income, savings, property, or family sponsorship, making residential security conditional

family_continuity.value: return-oriented systems become less viable when families and adult children have established long-term lives in the Gulf

observations.method: Focused policy and family-life-course analysis; the source does not estimate post-retirement healthcare use, eviction, visa denial, or return rates at population scale.
observations.uncertainty: Healthcare, housing and residence rules vary by country, visa category, employer, income, family composition and individual health; the source does not offer a uniform Gulf-wide outcome estimate.
observations.subgroup: Older migrant workers, spouses, adult children born or raised in the Gulf, lower-income retirees, people with chronic illness, renters, and families without secure residence status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some retirees may have sufficient savings, property, family sponsorship, or return options; staying in the Gulf is not necessarily the preferred or safest outcome for every household.

observations.period: 2026; policy responses to long-term migration and ageing

denominator.unit: ILO STREAM policy-response set for the South Asia–GCC corridor

proposed_protection.value: the paper calls for approaches that move beyond return-oriented models toward income security, affordable healthcare, housing, secure residence, and portable social protection

financing.value: a contributory social-protection fund is identified as one possible route to strengthen later-life security

coordination.value: destination and origin countries need stronger coordination because workers’ lives, contributions, families, care needs, and retirement decisions cross borders

programme_scope.value: the STREAM programme aims to expand inclusive, gender-responsive, rights-based social protection for migrant workers and families across the corridor

observations.method: Policy recommendations from an independent research paper within an ILO-supported programme; they are not adopted reforms or impact findings.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not establish fiscal feasibility, political adoption, contribution rates, benefit adequacy, portability administration, or whether the proposed reforms would change later-life outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Origin and destination governments, migrant workers, employers, social-protection agencies, health and housing providers, families, trade unions, and cross-border administrative institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A new cross-border fund or residence route could create contribution burdens, new eligibility exclusions, administrative complexity, or political resistance while leaving informal and undocumented workers outside coverage.

related_sources.claim: Official ILO research-repository record for the 2026 paper and abstract.
UN India republication of the ILO article summarizing the retirement-income, healthcare, housing, residence and portability gaps.

boundary: This record adds a migration life-course and social-protection portability route: temporary labour migration can become long-term residence and multigenerational family life, exposing gaps in retirement income, healthcare, housing, residency and cross-border benefit continuity. It is a focused qualitative research and policy synthesis centred on Indian families in the UAE, not representative Gulf-wide prevalence, causal evidence, a complete pension account, or proof that proposed reforms have been adopted or would work.
